title: Measurability through a countable test family
promptMarkdown:
Let $(X,\mathcal M)$ be a measurable space.

1. Prove that $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ is measurable if and only if $\{f>q\}\in\mathcal M$ for every **rational** $q$.
2. Let $X$ be uncountable and let $\mathcal M_c$ be the countable–co-countable σ-algebra of exercise 1. Prove that $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is $\mathcal M_c$-measurable if and only if there is a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ such that $\{x\in X: f(x)\neq c\}$ is countable.
3. Let $f_n:X\to\mathbb R$ be $\mathcal M_c$-measurable and suppose $f_n\to f$ pointwise on $X$. Theorem 0.3 of lecture 2 says that $f$ is measurable; confirm this directly from your characterisation in part 2, identifying the constant for $f$ in terms of the constants $c_n$ for the $f_n$.
hintLadder: Every real $\alpha$ is approached by rationals from above: express $\{f>\alpha\}$ as a countable union of sets $\{f>q\}$ with $q$ rational, then apply the $(\alpha,\infty]$ criterion.

For the easy direction of part 2, split according to whether $c\in U$. For the hard direction, for each rational $q$ the set $\{f\le q\}$ is countable or co-countable; let $S$ be the set of rationals $q$ for which it is countable.

Show that $S$ is a down-set of $\mathbb Q$ (if $q\in S$ and $q'<q$ then $q'\in S$), that $S\neq\mathbb Q$ and that $S\neq\emptyset$, using that $X$ is uncountable and $f$ is real-valued. Then let $c=\sup S$ and examine $\{f<c\}$ and $\{f>c\}$.
For part 3, the exceptional sets $N_n=\{f_n\neq c_n\}$ are countable; what happens to $f_n(x)$ for $x$ outside their union, and why is that union not all of $X$?

deterministicChecks.description: the characterisation of M_c-measurable functions names a constant value taken off a countable set

criteria.criterion: {f > α} is written as a countable union of sets {f > q} over rationals q > α, and the (α, ∞] criterion is invoked.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Union identity justified in both directions and the criterion cited.

criteria.criterion: Measurable ⇒ constant off a countable set: a correct argument locating the constant (for instance via the down-set S = {q ∈ ℚ : {f ≤ q} countable}, shown nonempty and proper using that X is uncountable, and c = sup S), with both {f < c} and {f > c} shown countable.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Constant located, both tails countable, uncountability of X used explicitly.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Right idea; one tail or the nonemptiness/properness of S not justified.

criteria.criterion: Constant off a countable set ⇒ measurable, by the case split c ∈ U or c ∉ U.

Part 3: off the countable union of the exceptional sets the functions are constants c_n, the limit forces (c_n) to converge (the complement is nonempty because X is uncountable), and f equals lim c_n off a countable set.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Union of exceptional sets, convergence of c_n justified, constant identified.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Constant identified but convergence of c_n or nonemptiness of the complement not justified.

levels.label: not met
levels.description: Missing or appeals only to Theorem 0.3.

checkExamples.label: characterisation stated
checkExamples.text: Claim: f is M_c-measurable if and only if f is constant outside a countable set. If f = c off a countable set N, then for any U either c ∈ U, so the preimage contains X \ N and is co-countable, or c ∉ U, so the preimage lies inside N and is countable.

checkExamples.label: no characterisation
checkExamples.text: f is measurable iff the preimage of every open set is countable or co-countable; this is just the definition, so there is nothing more to say.
